slides.headline:
The address already
tells you where it is.
slides.subline: A Korean street number is a coordinate, not a label. Three rules and you can walk straight to the place

slides.label: Multiply a building number on a -daero or -ro by about ten and you get roughly how many metres it sits from the start of that road
slides.note: Anyang City's own worked example: Simin-daero runs from number 1 to number 423, and the road is about 4.23 km long · Sources: Anyang City, Hanam City, juso.go.kr · Checked 24 October 2026

slides.title:
Every road is
a number line.
slides.body:
A Korean road is measured from a fixed start point, and the direction is set by rule: west to east, south to north. Numbers are then laid down the road at 20-metre intervals — odd on your left, even on your right, as you walk from that start point.

So the number is a distance, not a position in a queue. Two consecutive numbers sit about 10 metres apart on opposite sides, which is where the ×10 shortcut comes from. On a narrow -gil the steps are tighter, roughly half that, because the interval can be set under 20 metres.

items.d: A -daero is 8 lanes or more, a -ro is 2 to 7 lanes, and a -gil is everything smaller. The suffix alone says whether you are heading for a boulevard or an alley

items.t: The number in an alley name is the useful part
items.d: An alley is named after its parent road. 'Anyang-ro 398-beon-gil' is the alley that branches off Anyang-ro at number 398 — so about 3.98 km along it

items.t: Look for 번 (beon). It changes the meaning
items.d: With 번, the number is a distance. Without it — Seoul's usual form, like Dapsimni-ro 23-gil — it simply counts the side streets in branching order, odd to the left and even to the right

items.t: A hyphen means same spot, next door
items.d: 12-1 and 12-2 are separate buildings sharing one 20-metre interval, numbered by their main entrances. A further alley off an alley adds 가, 나, 다

items.t: Pick your side before you start walking
items.d: Odd and even sit on opposite sides of the road. Checking whether your number is odd or even halves the search before you take a step

items.t: Let the number tell you how far
items.d: Number 18 is near the top of the road; number 320 is a 3-kilometre walk from it. If the count is rising as you walk, you are going the right way

items.t: Old lot numbers are still everywhere
items.d: Road-name addresses have been the only legal ones since 1 January 2014, but jibeon lot numbers survive in property records and casual use. Map apps take both; the two do not convert by arithmetic
Street plates show the numbers covered by that stretch, so a plate reading 1→423 is telling you the road's whole span. Read it before you commit to a direction

slides.text:
It is a rule of thumb,
not a map. Know which
half you are standing in.
slides.by: The ×10 trick is an approximation. Numbers are assigned to the road at fixed intervals rather than to buildings, so gaps, infill and odd-shaped plots all bend the arithmetic — and Seoul's plain -gil names carry no distance at all, only a count. The method that works in Anyang will quietly mislead you in Jongno. This post is research, not a personal visit. Every rule here comes from a published government source, checked on 24 October 2026.

caption:
Korean addresses look like a wall of unfamiliar words, and most visitors give up and follow the blue dot. That is a shame, because the address is already telling you where the place is — it just encodes it as a distance rather than a name.

Here is the system. Every road has a fixed start point, with the direction set by rule: west to east, south to north. Numbers are then laid along it at 20-metre intervals, odd numbers on the left and even on the right as you walk from that start. Because the two sides alternate, consecutive numbers sit roughly 10 metres apart — which is why multiplying a building number on a -daero or -ro by about ten gives you its rough distance in metres from the start of the road. Anyang City uses its own street to demonstrate it: Simin-daero runs from number 1 to number 423, and the road is about 4.23 km long. On a narrow -gil the steps are tighter, roughly half that, because the interval can be set under 20 metres.

The suffix is doing work too. A -daero is eight lanes or more, a -ro is two to seven, and a -gil is everything smaller, so the name alone tells you whether you are heading for a boulevard or a back alley. And when an alley is named after its parent road, look closely for 번 (beon). 'Anyang-ro 398-beon-gil' branches off Anyang-ro at number 398, about 3.98 km along it. But Seoul mostly uses the other form: in a name like Dapsimni-ro 23-gil there is no 번, and the number is not a distance at all — it just counts the side streets in branching order, odd ones to the left and even ones to the right. Same-looking name, completely different meaning. Hyphens, meanwhile, mean neighbours: 12-1 and 12-2 are separate buildings sharing one interval.

Two honest caveats. Numbers are assigned to the road rather than to buildings, so gaps and infill bend the arithmetic — treat it as a rule of thumb, not a map. And old jibeon lot numbers are still everywhere, in property records and in everyday speech, even though road-name addresses have been the only legal ones since 1 January 2014; map apps accept both, but the two systems do not convert by arithmetic. Know which half you are standing in and you will find the restaurant. Sources in the last slide.
